extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent applicants/patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examination focusing on standards for asserted utility (especially therapeutic/pharmacological utilities), evidentiary sufficiency, and rules for inventorship and claim interpretation under the MPEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of evidence for asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The character and amount of evidence needed to support an asserted utility will vary depending on what is claimed and whether the asserted utility appears to contravene established principles and beliefs. An applicant does not have to provide evidence 'beyond a reasonable doubt' or establish utility as a matter of statistical certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence will be sufficient if, considered as a whole, it leads a person of ordinary skill in the art to conclude that the asserted utility is more likely than not true. (Cited cases: Ex parte Ferguson; In re Gazave; In re Irons; Nelson v. Bowler.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Special consideration for therapeutic or pharmacological utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should be particularly careful when reviewing evidence supporting asserted therapeutic or pharmacological utilities; evidence of pharmacological or other biological activity is relevant if there is a reasonable correlation between the activity and the asserted therapeutic use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant may establish reasonable correlation by statistically relevant data, arguments or reasoning, documentary evidence (e.g., scientific articles), or any combination. The applicant does not have to prove correlation with statistical certainty nor provide human success evidence; all that is required is a reasonable correlation. (Cited cases: Cross v. Iizuka; In re Jolles; Nelson v. Bowler.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural similarity to compounds with established utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of structural similarity to a compound known to have a particular therapeutic or pharmacological utility may support an assertion of therapeutic utility for a new compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should evaluate not only the existence of the structural relationship but also the reasoning used by the applicant or declarant to explain why that structural similarity is relevant to the asserted utility. Structural similarity presented together with substantial activity (e.g., animal screening) should be given appropriate weight. (Example: In re Jolles.)

rubrics_metrics.name: In vitro or animal testing generally sufficient to support therapeutic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: If reasonably correlated to the particular therapeutic utility, data from in vitro assays, animal models, or a combination will almost invariably be sufficient to establish therapeutic or pharmacological utility for a compound, composition or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must evaluate factors a person of ordinary skill would consider predictive: test parameters, choice of animal, relationship of activity to the disorder, compound characteristics, relative significance of the data, and applicant's explanation. Absence of certification that a test is an industry-accepted model is not dispositive. If the data supplied is consistent with the asserted utility, the Office cannot maintain a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101. (Cited cases: In re Brana; Cross v. Iizuka; In re Jolles; Ex parte Maas; Ex parte Balzarini.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Human clinical data not required to establish utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should not impose on applicants the unnecessary burden of providing evidence from human clinical trials to establish utility for inventions related to treatment of human disorders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No decisional law requires human clinical trial data to establish utility; courts have not required such data even where no animal models exist. If an applicant has initiated human clinical trials, examiners should generally presume the applicant has established the subject matter is reasonably predictive of the asserted therapeutic utility. (Cited cases: In re Isaacs; In re Langer; Ex parte Balzarini.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and efficacy evidence outside PTO remit
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office must confine its review of patent applications to statutory patent requirements and should not request evidence of safety in humans or regarding degree of effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other agencies (e.g., FDA) have responsibility for safety/efficacy standards; FDA review may provide a rationale for an asserted utility but FDA approval is not a prerequisite for patentability. If FDA experts have assessed and found a rationale satisfactory for a use that is set forth in the specification, Office personnel must be extremely hesitant to challenge utility and must be able to carry their burden to show no sound rationale exists. (Cited cases: In re Brana; Scott v. Finney.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of specific disease conditions — credibility varies
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to treating or curing diseases with no previously successful treatments warrant careful review; credibility of asserted utility may be more difficult when current scientific understanding suggests the task is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of known cure is not automatically a basis to find lack of utility. An assertion of usefulness for treating a symptom may be credible with modest evidence, whereas an assertion of 'curing' the disease may require significantly greater evidentiary support. Expert affidavits indicating reasonable expectation of success, supported by sound reasoning, usually should be sufficient to establish credibility. (Cited cases: In re Jolles; In re Buting; In re Sichert; citations to FDA regulations 21 CFR 312.80-88.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship: naming and oath/declaration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor, or each joint inventor, must be identified and must execute an oath or declaration directed to the application (with specific procedures for pre- and post-September 16, 2012 filings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign applicants may misunderstand U.S. inventorship naming requirements; a request under 37 CFR 1.48 is required to correct inventorship errors. For pre-September 16, 2012 applications, the party executing the oath/declaration is presumed to be the inventor. See MPEP § 602.01 and related sections for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must contribute to the conception of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The threshold question for inventorship is who conceived the invention; unless a person contributes to conception, he/she is not an inventor. Reduction to practice is irrelevant except in simultaneity situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person who shares in conception is a joint inventor. General knowledge about biological properties or suggesting only a desired result (rather than the means to accomplish it) is insufficient to confer inventorship. (Cited authorities: In re Hardee; In re VerHoef; Board of Education ex rel. FSU v. American Bioscience Inc.; Ex parte Smernoff.) See MPEP sections on evidence required to establish conception or reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor not required to personally reduce the invention to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor need not themselves reduce the invention to practice; reduction to practice done on inventor's behalf is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation of steps that do not require exercise of inventive skill does not make the implementer an inventor; a technician following instructions is generally not an inventor. (Cited cases: Fritsch v. Lin; In re DeBaun; Mattor v. Coolegem; Tucker v. Naito.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint inventorship — scope and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention is made by two or more persons jointly, they shall apply for patent jointly and each make the required oath; joint inventors may not have worked together or at the same time, may have different types or amounts of contribution, and need not have contributed to every claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'quantum of collaboration or connection' is required — e.g., collaboration, working under common direction, one inventor seeing a report and building on it, or hearing another's suggestion. Contribution to at least one claim suffices for joint inventorship. The contributor of a disclosed means for a means-plus-function element can be a joint inventor as to that claim. (Cited authorities: 35 U.S.C. 116; Kimberly-Clark Corp. v. Procter & Gamble; Ethicon Inc. v. United States Surgical Corp.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship for continuing applications claiming 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: An application claiming the benefit of a prior filed copending application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application; the earlier application must disclose the named inventor's invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So long as at least one inventor is common and other requirements are met, the Office will permit a 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit claim without additional submissions. Examiners must check the earlier application to determine common inventorship and compliance with 35 U.S.C. 120 and 37 CFR 1.78; benefit may be permitted without examining the earlier application for disclosure/support unless necessary (e.g., intervening reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation (BROI) in light of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: During patent examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification, as would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO determines claim scope not solely on claim language but by giving claims their broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification (37 CFR 1.75(d)(1)). Examiners use BROI during prosecution to establish a clear record of applicant intent; courts interpret claims differently in infringement/validity proceedings with a fully developed record. (Cited cases: Phillips v. AWH Corp.; In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr.; In re Suitco Surface; In re Morris.)
